Impatient describes a feeling of not being able to wait calmly. When you are impatient, something inside you is pushing, pulling, or rushing — you want something to happen now, or you want a delay or difficulty to stop, and the waiting or the slowness is causing you discomfort, restlessness, or irritation.

Think of it this way: patience is the ability to stay calm while waiting or while dealing with something difficult or slow. Impatient is simply the opposite of that. The prefix "im-" means "not," so impatient = not patient.
The Two Main Flavours of Impatient

This word carries two closely related but slightly different feelings, and understanding both is key.

1. Impatient because you are eager or excited

Here, impatience is driven by positive energy — you want something so much that waiting feels almost unbearable, even though you're not necessarily angry. You're restless, buzzing, and time feels like it's moving too slowly.

  • A child on the night before a birthday is impatient for the morning to arrive.
  • A student who has worked hard is impatient to hear their exam results.
  • A traveller standing at the boarding gate is impatient to board the plane.

In these cases, impatient is very close in feeling to "eager" or "anxious with excitement." The waiting itself is the problem, not the person or situation causing it.

2. Impatient because you are irritated or frustrated

Here, impatience comes from a negative place — you're annoyed, frustrated, or intolerant. Something or someone is moving too slowly, making mistakes, or taking too long, and it is getting on your nerves.

  • A manager who keeps sighing and checking their watch during a long meeting is impatient.
  • A driver who honks aggressively at slow traffic is showing impatience.
  • Someone who interrupts others before they finish speaking may be doing so because they are impatient.
Impatient as a Permanent Trait vs. a Temporary Feeling

One useful distinction: impatient can describe either a fleeting moment or a character trait.

As a temporary feeling (a state in the moment):

  • "She became impatient after waiting an hour for the bus."
  • "He was impatient during the long speech."

As a permanent personality trait (a general tendency):

  • "My grandfather was always an impatient man — he hated waiting for anything."
  • "She is impatient by nature; she likes things done immediately."

When you call someone an impatient person, you mean they regularly and habitually struggle to wait or stay calm — it's a part of who they are.
How Impatient Is Used With Different Prepositions

The word "impatient" pairs with certain prepositions, and each pairing gives a slightly different meaning.

Impatient + to + verb — You desperately want to do something and can't wait to do it.

  • "She was impatient to open her gift."
  • "He is impatient to get started."

Impatient + for + noun — You are waiting eagerly or restlessly for something.

  • "The crowd was impatient for the concert to begin."
  • "Everyone is impatient for an answer."

Impatient + with + person or thing — You are irritated or intolerant of someone or something.

  • "He is impatient with people who talk too slowly."
  • "She gets impatient with technology when it doesn't work properly."
What Impatience Looks and Sounds Like in Real Life

Understanding impatience is easier when you picture it. An impatient person might:

  • Tap their fingers on a table, or tap their foot on the floor.
  • Sigh loudly and repeatedly.
  • Keep checking the time.
  • Interrupt someone mid-sentence.
  • Finish other people's sentences for them.
  • Say things like "Come on!", "Hurry up!", or "How long is this going to take?"
  • Speak in a sharp, snappy tone.
  • Pace around while waiting.

These are all outward signs of the inner restlessness and discomfort that impatience creates.
Impatient Can Describe People, Actions, and Even Gestures

"Impatient" doesn't only describe a person — it can describe specific actions or physical gestures that show impatience.

  • "She gave an impatient sigh." (The sigh itself shows her impatience.)
  • "He made an impatient gesture with his hand, urging her to hurry."
  • "There was an impatient knock at the door — fast, sharp, repeated."

In all these cases, the word is pointing to something being done in a way that reveals inner restlessness or irritation.
Degree and Intensity

Impatience can be mild or strong, and you can describe the degree:

  • Slightly impatient — just a little restless, barely noticeable.
  • Growing impatient — the feeling is building as time goes on.
  • Visibly impatient — you can clearly see it on the person's face or body.
  • Deeply / thoroughly impatient — a strong, intense feeling, very hard to suppress.
Synonyms — and How They Differ

These words are close to "impatient" but not identical:

Restless — You can't sit still and feel unsettled, but it's not always because of waiting. Restless is broader.

Eager — You desperately want something, but eager doesn't carry the irritation or discomfort that impatient does. You can be eager and perfectly calm.

Anxious — You're nervous or worried about something, which may overlap with impatience, but anxious is more about fear and worry.

Irritable — You're easily annoyed and snappy in general, not necessarily because of waiting.

Intolerant — You have no patience for certain things or people — this overlaps with the "impatient with" usage, but intolerant is stronger and broader.

None of these fully replace "impatient." Impatient is specific: it always involves the struggle to wait or endure something, combined with restlessness or irritation.
Antonyms — The Opposite End

Patient is the direct opposite — staying calm while waiting, enduring delays without frustration.

Tolerant, composed, calm, and unhurried are also on the opposite end of the scale.
Other Forms of the Word

Knowing how the word changes form will help you recognise it everywhere:

  • The adjective: impatient — "She was impatient."
  • The adverb: impatiently — "He waited impatiently." (in an impatient manner)
  • The noun: impatience — "Her impatience was obvious to everyone." (the state or quality of being impatient)
A Quick Summary to Lock It In

Impatient means unable or unwilling to wait calmly. It describes the restlessness, irritation, or eager discomfort you feel when something is taking too long, when someone is moving too slowly, or when you want something to happen right now and it isn't. It can describe a fleeting feeling in the moment, or a lasting part of someone's character. It can be positive-flavoured (excited, eager) or negative-flavoured (irritated, intolerant), but in both cases, the core is the same: the inability to wait with calm and ease.
